title: Transverse momentum as the counter-diabatic generator in bent waveguide couplers
abstract: Bending the axis of a mode-evolution coupler suppresses the nonadiabatic coupling between its supermodes, and bent couplers of this kind were recently shown to realize the counter-diabatic (CD) protocol. Here we identify the operator responsible. Rigid lateral displacement of a waveguide structure is generated by the transverse momentum $\hat p_x$, whose diagonal matrix elements vanish in a real supermode basis and whose off-diagonal element is purely imaginary; in a two-mode system such an operator is proportional to $\sy$. The CD term of a two-waveguide coupler is itself proportional to $\sy$, while the detuning and the coupling, the two parameters set by the waveguide widths and spacing, lie in the $σ_z$--$σ_x$ plane and cannot produce it. The transverse momentum is therefore the CD generator of the bent coupler, by necessity rather than by design. Equating the term it supplies to the nonadiabatic coupling gives the axis slope in closed form as a ratio of two matrix elements of the unperturbed supermodes at a single cross section, which a commutator identity recasts in coupled-mode variables as $\dot{\xo}=\dotθ/(γ\dbeta^{2})$. The expression agrees with the numerical offset search to $0.3\%$ and requires no search. Beam propagation simulations confirm the design and compare it, for the first time, with the CD protocol realized by unitary transformation in a straight coupler built from the same reference structure. The two devices reach $0.994$ and $1.000$ supermode fidelity where the untreated coupler reaches $0.886$, and agree in bandwidth and fabrication tolerance, while their internal trajectories differ by exactly the frame transformation that relates them.
summary: This paper analyzes mode-evolution couplers, demonstrating that achieving perfect adiabatic light transfer requires a Counter-Diabatic (CD) driving term. The authors prove that the transverse momentum ($\hat{p}_x$) supplies this necessary term when the coupler axis is bent. This allows them to analytically design the required bending profile, achieving high supermode fidelity comparable to other advanced control methods.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of achieving high-fidelity, fast mode conversion in optical couplers by implementing the Counter-Diabatic (CD) protocol.
main_result: The transverse momentum ($\hat{p}_x$) is identified as the necessary and sufficient generator for the CD term in bent waveguide couplers, allowing for an analytical determination of the required axis slope.
method: The authors use a Hamiltonian approach, comparing the required CD term ($\propto \sigma_y$) with the terms available from geometric control ($\Delta, \Omega$), and deriving the required spatial profile from the momentum operator.
model_or_system: The system is a two-mode optical coupler governed by coupled-mode equations analogous to the time-dependent Schrödinger equation. The evolution is analyzed using supermode basis states, with the Hamiltonian depending on detuning ($\Delta$) and coupling ($\Omega$).
key_observables: Supermode fidelity ($P_+$), which quantifies the efficiency of light transfer, and the required axis slope $\dot{x}_0(z)$.
important_parameters: The rate of change of the mixing angle ($\dot{	heta}$), the supermode splitting ($\Delta eta$), and the geometric parameters ($\Delta, \Omega$).
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to a two-level approximation and is derived assuming the coupling mechanism is dominated by the transverse momentum's effect.
figures_summary: Figures compare the supermode fidelity for three coupler types (untreated, gauge realization, bent realization) under fabrication errors, showing the bent realization achieves near-unity fidelity.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the need for a CD term ($\propto \sigma_y$) that cannot be generated by standard geometric parameters ($\Delta, \Omega$). It then demonstrates that transverse momentum ($\hat{p}_x$) supplies this term, leading to a closed-form expression for the required axis slope, which is verified against numerical simulations.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, physical realization of a theoretical concept (CD driving) in a photonic system, showing how geometric manipulation (bending) can compensate for nonadiabatic losses, which is highly relevant to quantum optics and integrated photonics.
